- Drafts only; nothing is published from this workspace. Save to /workspace/out/. Questions go to the requester.

# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

New Research on Mass Shootings: Banning Large-Capacity Magazines Substantially Lowers Fatalities 

 New Research on Mass Shootings: Banning Large-Capacity Magazines Substantially Lowers Fatalities

 Skip to content 
 Skip to primary navigation 
 Skip to search box 
 Skip to admissions quick links 
 Skip to secondary navigation 
 Skip to breadcrumb 

 States that ban large-capacity magazines (LCMs)—detachable ammunition feeding devices that hold more than 10 bullets—experience substantially fewer high-fatality mass shootings than states that do not ban LCMs, according to a new study led by researchers at Teachers College and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

 The study finds that high-fatality mass shootings—defined as six or more fatal victims, not including the perpetrators—occurred in states that do not restrict ownership and possession of LCMs at a rate that was more than double the rate for states that do restrict LCMs. In addition, deaths in high-fatality mass shootings, relative to the population, were more than three times higher in states that did not restrict LCMs.

 LCM bans seek to lower the frequency and lethality of mass shootings. The study finds that LCM bans appear to be saving lives. The rationale behind LCM bans is that, if gunmen are forced interrupt their attacks more frequently in order to reload due to lower ammunition capacity, those precious seconds can allow potential victims in the line of fire to run, hide, or fight back—three widely prescribed life-saving tactics for surviving an active shooting.

 “Think back to the 2011 rampage in Tucson that targeted the crowd at a political meet-and-greet hosted by former Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords,” said TC research professor Louis Klarevas, lead author of the study. “The gunman in that attack used a handgun armed with a 33-round magazine to kill six and wound another 13, including Rep. Giffords. The casualty toll would certainly have been higher had the gunman not been tackled while switching out one large-capacity magazine for another. But by the same reasoning, the casualty toll would have been lower had the gunman been tackled after emptying a much smaller 10-round magazine. Imagine how many victims would have been spared if the gunman had fired 23 fewer bullets that day.”

 TC research professor Louis Klarevas, lead author of the study. Photo courtesy of Louis Klarevas. 

 In the last five years, high-fatality mass shootings have been occurring at a rate of more than four incidents per year. Approximately half of these attacks, prominent among them the massacres in Orlando, Las Vegas, and Sutherland Springs, claimed 10 or more lives. When perpetrators of high-fatality mass shootings used LCMs, their attacks resulted in a 62-percent higher average death toll.

 The study analyzed the time period from 1990-2017. The researchers selected 1990 as the starting point because, that year, New Jersey became the first state to restrict LCMs. Since then, eight other states plus the District of Columbia have enacted bans on LCMs. From September 1994 until September 2004, the possession or sale of new LCMs was prohibited nationwide by the federal assault weapons ban. That law expired in 2004, after Congress opted not to renew it.

 The study finds that the 1994 federal ban appears to have been effective in reducing mass shooting violence. Yet, even without a nationwide ban in place, states that tightly restricted LCMs still experienced high-fatality mass shootings at a lower rate than states that did not restrict LCMs.

 It seems that when LCMs are legal and available, they are more likely to be acquired and used by mass murderers. Nevertheless, since some potential shooters may import LCMs into states where they are prohibited, restricting LCMs across all 50 states promises a more effective way to reduce deaths associated with mass shootings.

 “Whether or not to ban large-capacity magazines is at the heart of the national debate over how to reduce gun violence,” Klarevas added. “Our research suggests that imposing tight restrictions on LCMs offers a practical legislative solution for helping to safeguard Americans from the threat of mass shootings.”

 The study,  “The Effect of Large-Capacity Magazine Bans on High-Fatality Mass Shootings, 1990-2017,” will appear in the December 2019 issue of the American Journal of Public Health , and published online on October 17, 2019. Andrew Conner, a medical student at the Frank H. Netter, MD, School of Medicine, Quinnipiac University, was a co-author.

 Gun Violence Widely Viewed as a Major – and Growing – National Problem 

 1. Views of U.S. gun laws, impact of gun ownership on safety 

 2. Americans’ views of specific gun policy proposals 

 Acknowledgments 

 Methodology 

 Several policy proposals that would further restrict access to guns or ammunition continue to receive support from majorities of Americans. Smaller shares of Americans support several more permissive policy proposals.

 Roughly nine-in-ten U.S. adults (88%) favor preventing people with mental illness from purchasing guns, while 79% favor increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old.

 Sizable majorities also support banning high-capacity ammunition magazines that hold more than 10 rounds (66%) and banning assault-style weapons (64%).

 Four policy proposals that would ease restrictions on guns, including allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit, draw less support from the public.

 Half of Americans favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools, while 44% say people should be able to carry concealed guns in more places. Fewer than a third of Americans favor shortening waiting periods for gun purchases (30%) or allowing concealed carry without a permit (24%).

 Views by party

 Overwhelming majorities of both Democrats (89%) and Republicans (88%) favor preventing people with mental illnesses from purchasing guns. Majorities in both parties support increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old, though support for this policy is more widespread among Democrats (90%) than Republicans (69%).

 There are wider partisan differences on the other policy proposals in the survey. While large majorities of Democrats favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (85%) and banning assault-style weapons (85%), fewer than half of Republicans support either of these two proposals (45% and 42%, respectively).

 By contrast, while seven-in-ten or more Republicans favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools (74%) or allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places (71%), fewer than three-in-ten Democrats support these policies. Republicans are also more likely than Democrats to favor shortening waiting periods for people who want to buy guns legally (45% vs. 16%) and allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit (40% vs. 9%), though both of these proposals have more opposition than support among those in both parties.

 Views of gun policies among gun owners, non-owners

 While nearly nine-in-ten gun owners (87%) and non-owners (89%) both favor preventing people with mental illnesses from purchasing guns, there are wider gaps between gun owners and non-owners on other policy proposals.

 Non-owners are at least 30 percentage points more likely than gun owners to favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (78% vs. 45%) or banning assault-style weapons (77% vs. 43%). They are also 18 points more likely to favor increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old, though majorities in both groups favor this (86% vs. 68%).

 Gun owners are 37 points more likely than non-owners to favor allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places (68% vs. 31%), and 30 points more likely to favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools (69% vs. 39%).

 Few non-owners favor shortened waiting periods (22%) or allowing concealed carry without a permit (14%). Gun owners are more supportive of these policies, with 44% favoring shorter waiting periods for people who want to buy guns legally and 41% supporting allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit. Still, majorities of gun owners oppose these policy proposals.

 Gun owners’, non-owners’ views by political party

 Across seven of the eight policy proposals asked about in the survey, gun owners within each political party are more likely than non-owners of the same party to favor policies that expand access to guns and ammunition.

 Non-owners are more likely to favor policies that are more restrictive – though differences are generally larger among Republicans and Republican leaners than among Democrats and Democratic leaners.

 At the same time, the wide partisan differences on these questions are seen among both gun owners and non-owners (Two-in-ten Democrats and 45% of Republicans say they personally own a gun).

 For example, nearly nine-in-ten Democrats who do not own a gun favor banning high-capacity magazines (89%), a view held by a smaller – though still wide – majority of Democrats who report owning a gun (73%). Meanwhile, a narrower majority of Republicans who do not own a gun (60%) favor this policy, compared with roughly half as many Republican gun owners (31%).

 A large majority of Republicans who own guns (85%) favor allowing teachers to carry guns in K-12 schools, as do 64% of Republicans who do not own a gun. Among Democrats, 34% of gun owners favor this, as do 25% of non-owners.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute
By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll on record. For the fourth year in a row, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- Federal law leaves the door open, and people are dying through it: 22% of Americans who acquired a firearm in the prior two years got it with no background check, and half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- The evidence of what works is in. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in gun homicide rates, and mass-shooting deaths were 70% less likely during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should close the gaps.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun every 11 minutes. The final count was 46,728 lives, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data. Those deaths happened in every kind of community: on city blocks and in suburban kitchens, at schools and workplaces and family gatherings. This is not a spike or an aberration. It is a sustained, man-made epidemic that federal policy continues to tolerate. The overall toll has stayed near record highs for five years, and no state has been left untouched. An epidemic that kills more than 46,000 people a year demands a federal response of the same scale.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll is not abstract. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer, according to CDC data for 2023. In that single year, gunfire took 2,566 young lives, an average of seven children and teens every day. A leading cause of death that is also preventable is a policy choice. Congress has the tools to change it.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check for sales by licensed firearms dealers. But the Brady framework stops at the storefront. In most states, a private sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no records and no questions. ...

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield**, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth straight year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- The gaps in federal law are measurable and deadly. An estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years did so with no background check, and about half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- We know what works. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in gun homicide rates, and mass-shooting deaths were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, an American was killed with a gun. By year's end the count stood at 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is a mass casualty event's worth of Americans every few days, sustained year after year in every kind of community: in homes, at schools, in workplaces, at grocery stores and birthday parties. It is not a spike. It is a steady, preventable loss on a scale no other high-income country tolerates. The overall toll has held near record highs for years, with no state untouched. An epidemic of this scale demands a federal response of the same size.

## 2. Children and teens

The harshest measure of this failure is written in the country's obituary pages. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses. A preventable cause of death holding first place among the young is not fate. It is the predictable result of federal law that lets guns move to the wrong hands through two open doors: the background-check gap and the legal market for assault weapons.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a sale by a licensed firearms dealer. The Brady framework stops at the storefront door. In most states, sales arranged online, at gun shows or between strangers can proceed with no check and no record.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of this gap at 22%: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years reported getting it with no background check, according to the 2017 Annals of Internal Medicine study by Miller, Hepburn and Azrael. Among private sales, the share without a check is about 50%. In a country where 46,728 people died of gunfire in a single year, that gap is not a technicality. It is the point of entry for guns that end up in the hands of people the law already says should not have them.

State experience proves the checks are worth running. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check on every handgun sale, was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable change in nonfirearm homicides. Congress would not be legislating blind. Americans, meanwhile, are far ahead of their representatives: 86% of adults support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, and polls have consistently found majorities of gun owners and Republicans on board.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and wounded 2,692 more. The country knows these events by place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the gunman was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the shooter fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of any type account for a small share of overall gun homicides, 2.6% in 2017 and 2.8% in 2018 in FBI data, but they dominate the nation's deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 high-fatality mass shootings documented between 1981 and 2017, 430, or 86%, were killed with assault rifles. The firepower itself sets the death toll: of 69 high-fatality mass shootings between 1990 and 2017, 64% involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, against 7 when the shooter did not have them. States without a ban on high-capacity magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with bans.

The federal government has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur than in the periods before and after it, and the ban period was associated with nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The ban expired in 2004. In the two decades since, Congress has watched the deadliest attacks on record accumulate and done nothing.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, online and gun-show loopholes that leave an estimated one in five recent acquisitions unchecked.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban, modernize its definitions to cover current variants, and restrict the high-capacity magazines that double and triple the death tolls documented in Section 4.

3. **Fund the science.** Provide sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, ending the Dickey-era freeze for good. ...

4. **Back state extreme-risk laws.** Offer federal grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders... In the two states studied first, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement began.

## Closing

There were 46,728 reasons in 2023 alone. The gaps in federal law have a body count...

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield**, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth straight year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- The gaps in federal law are measurable and deadly. An estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years did so with no background check, and about half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- We know what works. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in gun homicide rates, and mass-shooting deaths were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, an American was killed with a gun. By year's end the count stood at 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is a mass casualty event's worth of Americans every few days, sustained year after year in every kind of community: in homes, at schools, in workplaces, at grocery stores and birthday parties. It is not a spike. It is a steady, preventable loss on a scale no other high-income country tolerates. The overall toll has held near record highs for years, with no state untouched. An epidemic of this scale demands a federal response of the same size.

## 2. Children and teens

The harshest measure of this failure is written in the country's obituary pages. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses. A preventable cause of death holding first place among the young is not fate. It is the predictable result of federal law that lets guns move to the wrong hands through two open doors: the background-check gap and the legal market for assault weapons.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a sale by a licensed firearms dealer. The Brady framework stops at the storefront door. In most states, sales arranged online, at gun shows or between strangers can proceed with no check and no record.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of this gap at 22%: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years reported getting it with no background check, according to the 2017 Annals of Internal Medicine study by Miller, Hepburn and Azrael. Among private sales, the share without a check is about 50%. In a country where 46,728 people died of gunfire in a single year, that gap is not a technicality. It is the point of entry for guns that end up in the hands of people the law already says should not have them.

State experience proves the checks are worth running. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check on every handgun sale, was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable change in nonfirearm homicides. Congress would not be legislating blind. Americans, meanwhile, are far ahead of their representatives: 86% of adults support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, and polls have consistently found majorities of gun owners and Republicans on board.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and wounded 2,692 more. The country knows these events by place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the gunman was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the shooter fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of any type account for a small share of overall gun homicides, 2.6% in 2017 and 2.8% in 2018 in FBI data, but they dominate the nation's deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 high-fatality mass shootings documented between 1981 and 2017, 430, or 86%, were killed with assault rifles. The firepower itself sets the death toll: of 69 high-fatality mass shootings between 1990 and 2017, 64% involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, against 7 when the shooter did not have them. States without a ban on high-capacity magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with bans.

The federal government has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur than in the periods before and after it, and the ban period was associated with nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The ban expired in 2004. In the two decades since, Congress has watched the deadliest attacks on record accumulate and done nothing.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, online and gun-show loopholes that leave an estimated one in five recent acquisitions unchecked.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban, modernize its definitions to cover current variants, and restrict the high-capacity magazines that double and triple the death tolls documented in Section 4.

3. **Fund the science.** Provide sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, ending the Dickey-era freeze for good. ...

4. **Back state extreme-risk laws.** Offer federal grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders... In the two states studied first, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement began.

## Closing

There were 46,728 reasons in 2023 alone. The gaps in federal law have a body count...

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun. The final count was 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data.

That is a loss the country has learned to absorb rather than stop. It shows up in every kind of community: in homes and on city blocks, at schools and workplaces, at grocery stores, birthday parties and family celebrations. ## 2. Children and teens

The clearest measure of that failure is generational. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses, according to the CDC.

## 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every sale by a licensed firearms dealer since 1994. The Brady framework stops there. In most states, a sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no record and no questions.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield**, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Scheduled publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- The gaps in federal law are measurable and deadly. An estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no background check, and about half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- The evidence for action is in. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in the state's firearm homicide rate, and mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the decade the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should close both gaps, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun. The final count was 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data.

That is a loss the country has learned to absorb rather than stop. It shows up in every kind of community: in homes and on city blocks, at schools and workplaces, at grocery stores, birthday parties and family celebrations. The toll has held near record highs year after year, and it has touched every state. No other high-income country accepts anything like it, because none has to. Gun violence on this scale is not weather. It is the direct product of laws Congress wrote and laws Congress has declined to write.

## 2. Children and teens

The clearest measure of that failure is generational. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses, according to the CDC.

The country did not arrive here by accident. Two open doors in federal law put guns in the wrong hands: a background-check requirement that stops at the storefront, and a legal market, restored after 2004, for assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that make mass shootings deadlier.

## 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every sale by a licensed firearms dealer since 1994. The Brady framework stops there. In most states, a sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no record and no questions.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of this gap at 22%. In a 2017 national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check. Among private-party sales, roughly half involved no check. When 46,728 people are dying by gunfire in a year, that is not a technicality in the law. It is the on-ramp by which guns reach the very people the law says should not have them.

The checks work where they are actually required. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check on every handgun sale in the state, was followed by a 40% reduction in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable decline in nonfirearm homicides.

The public is not waiting to be persuaded. In the May 2023 Mood of the Nation poll, 86% of American adults, including clear majorities of Republicans and gun owners, favored requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers.

Hmm — "including clear majorities of Republicans and gun owners" — Mood of the Nation: is that verified for that poll? Not verified. Pew 2021: 70% of Republicans favored extending checks to private sales/gun shows. So: "In the May 2023 Mood of the Nation poll, 86% of American adults favored requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers. Pew found 81% overall support in April 2021, including 70% of Republicans." Verified. Use that.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023 the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. The country knows these events by place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the shooter was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of all kinds are used in a small share of the country's gun murders, 2.9% of them in 2018 in FBI data, but they are concentrated in the deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 high-fatality mass shootings recorded between 1981 and 2017, 430 were killed with assault rifles, 86% of the toll. The firepower drives the death count: of 69 high-fatality mass shootings between 1990 and 2017, 64% involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, compared with seven when the shooter did not have one. States without bans on the magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with them.

The federal government has run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than in the periods before and after, and the ban period accounted for nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The law expired in 2004. In the two decades since, as the evidence below shows, Congress has watched the record books fill and treated it as someone else's problem.

"mass shootings have increased more than 150 percent since 2013" (The Trace). Klarevas: high-fatality mass shootings occurring at a rate of more than four incidents per year in the last five years (as of 2019), and half claimed 10+ lives. ## 5. Recommendations

1. Pass universal background checks. Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online loopholes that leave an estimated 22% of recent acquisitions unchecked and roughly half of private sales without a check.

2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 ban's core protections, update its definitions to capture the variants marketed since 2004, and prohibit the high-capacity magazines that double and triple the lethality documented in high-fatality attacks.

3. Fund the science of gun violence prevention. Sustain and expand dedicated research funding at the CDC and NIH. Congress let a 20-year freeze end with a first $25 million appropriation in 2020; the country's third-deadliest year on record should have ended the era of underfunding for good.

4. Back state extreme-risk laws. Offer planning and implementation grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders, which let courts temporarily remove firearms from people found to be a danger to themselves or others. In the first two states studied, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement.

## Closing

There were 46,728 reasons in 2023 alone, and more every 11 minutes since. None of the gaps in federal law is a mystery...

"The gaps this brief describes are the result of choices Congress has made. In 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives, including 2,566 children and teens. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban are not radical proposals. They are policies the country has already tried, measured and found to work, and they command broad public support. The evidence is assembled. What is missing is the vote."

Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in the state's firearm homicide rate, and mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the decade the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the ban, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun. The final count was 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data.

Behind each of those numbers is a person: a parent at a kitchen table, a teenager at a bus stop, a coworker who did not come home. That is a loss the country has learned to absorb rather than stop. It shows up in every kind of community, in homes and on city blocks, at schools and workplaces, at grocery stores, birthday parties and family celebrations. The toll has held near record highs year after year, and it has touched every state. No comparable high-income country accepts anything like it, because none of them has to. Gun violence on this scale is not weather. It is the product of laws Congress wrote and of gaps Congress has declined to close.

## 2. Children and teens

The clearest measure of that failure is generational. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancers, according to the CDC.

The country did not arrive here by accident. Two open doors in federal law put guns in the wrong hands: a background-check requirement that stops at the storefront, and a legal market, restored after 2004, in assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that make mass shootings deadlier.

## 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every sale by a licensed firearms dealer since 1994. The Brady framework stops at the storefront door. In most states, a sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no record and no questions.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of that gap at 22%. In a national survey published in 2017 in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check. Among private-party sales, about half involved no check at all. In a country where 46,728 people died by gunfire in a single year, that gap is not a technicality. It is the on-ramp by which guns reach the very people the law already says should not have them.

A background check takes minutes, and it asks only whether the buyer falls into a category Congress has already barred from gun ownership: people convicted of serious crimes, domestic abusers and others the law disqualifies. The check is not an infringement on anyone Congress allows to own a gun. It is the system Congress built to enforce its own decisions, and it only works if it applies to every sale.

The checks work where they are actually required. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which places a background check on every handgun sale in the state, was followed by a 40% reduction in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable change in nonfirearm homicides.

The public is not waiting to be persuaded. In the May 2023 Mood of the Nation poll, 86% of American adults supported requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers. Pew Research Center found in April 2021 that 81% of Americans, including 70% of Republicans, favored extending checks to private sales and gun shows.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. The country knows these events by their place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the shooter was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of all kinds are used in a small share of the nation's gun murders, 2.9% of them in 2018 in FBI data, but they are concentrated in the deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 mass shootings with four or more fatalities recorded between 1981 and 2017, 430 were killed with assault rifles, 86% of the toll. The firepower drives the death count: of 69 mass shootings with six or more deaths between 1990 and 2017, 44 involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, compared with seven when the shooter did not have one. States without bans on the magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with them.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than in the periods before and after, and the ban period was associated with nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The law expired in 2004, and since then the annual count of mass shootings has more than doubled, from 255 in 2013 to 656 in 2023.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online loopholes that leave an estimated 22% of recent acquisitions unchecked and about half of private sales without a check.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's core protections, update its definitions to capture the variants marketed since 2004, and prohibit the high-capacity magazines that raise the average death toll in the deadliest attacks from seven victims to 12.

3. **Fund the science of gun safety.** Sustain and expand dedicated gun violence research funding at the CDC and the NIH. The first dedicated appropriation in more than two decades, $25 million for fiscal 2020, passed in December 2019, 23 years after the Dickey Amendment restricted federal gun violence research. A year in which 46,728 Americans die by gunfire should end that era of underfunding for good.

4. **Back state extreme-risk laws.** Provide planning and implementation grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people found to be a danger to themselves or others. In the first two states studied, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement began.

## Closing

The gaps this brief describes are the result of choices, and in 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives, including 2,566 children and teens. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban are not untested ideas. They are policies the country has already tried, measured and found to work, and they command broad public support. The evidence is assembled in this brief and its data appendix. What is missing is the vote.

---

*All figures in this brief, with full source lines and methodology notes, appear in the companion data appendix (data_appendix.md).*

{"path":"/workspace/out/data_appendix.md","content":"# Data appendix: Closing the gaps (Safer Communities Brief No. 9)

Northgate Progress Institute | Draft for editorial review | Companion to brief.md
All figures used in the brief appear below, one table per figure, with source lines and notes. Per the publications style sheet, intent breakdowns, age ranges, definitions and methodology notes live in this appendix, not in body copy, the fact sheet or the stat cards.

**Terminology (style sheet A2).** House style uses "assault weapons" for the category defined in the author's outline, i.e., the semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity magazines covered by the federal assault weapons ban of 1994 (Public Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act), which took effect in September 1994 and expired in September 2004. Cited studies use their own terms ("assault rifles," "high-capacity" or "large-capacity" magazines); original wording is preserved in the tables below.

## A1. U.S. firearm deaths, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Sections 1, 3 and 5; closing; fact sheet; stat card 1.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Total firearm deaths | 46,728 (third-highest annual total ever recorded) |
| Firearm suicides | 27,300 (58% of total; record high) |
| Firearm homicides | 17,927 |
| Frequency | One death every 11 minutes |

**Source:** CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 2023 final data, https://wonder.cdc.gov/, as compiled in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

**Notes (style sheet B2).** The headline toll in body copy is total gun deaths; the intent breakdown appears here. Suicides have been the majority of U.S. gun deaths every year since 1995. Firearm homicides declined from their pandemic-era peak of 20,958 (2021) and 19,651 (2022) to 17,927 (2023); the overall 2023 total was still the third-highest ever recorded, and total gun deaths remained near the record set in 2021. CDC final mortality data come from death certificates and are released with a lag, so 2023 is the most recent year of final data. Rates elsewhere in this appendix are per 100,000 U.S. residents.

## A2. Children and teens, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Section 2; closing; fact sheet; stat card 2.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Firearm deaths, ages 1-17, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Rate, ages 1-17 | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Leading cause of death for this age group | Fourth consecutive year |
| Intent breakdown | Homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined or other 3% |

**Source:** CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 2023 final data, https://wonder.cdc.gov/, as compiled in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

**Notes (style sheet B3).** Body copy follows house phrasing, "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; the age range is ages 1-17, and firearms accounted for more deaths in this group than car crashes, overdoses or cancers. "An average of seven young people every day" (Section 2) is a derivation: 2,566 deaths across 365 days. A separate pooled estimate for ages 1-19 (5.9 per 100,000, 2021-2023, America's Health Rankings) is in the source tables but was not used in copy; flag to research if the editor wants it included.

## A3. Firearm acquisitions without a background check
*Used in: executive summary; Section 3; Section 5, recommendation 1; fact sheet; stat card 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Owners who acquired a firearm in the prior 2 years without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16% to 27%) |
| Private-party purchases acquired without a check | ~50% |

**Source:** Miller M, Hepburn L, Azrael D, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, February 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590

**Notes (style sheet B4).** 2015 national probability-based survey of 1,613 gun owners; "recent acquisition" means the most recent firearm obtained within the previous two years. The 22% figure is the house estimate for copy. An older and frequently misused figure, from the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook and Ludwig), found about 40% of recently acquired guns had not gone through a licensed dealer; that estimate includes gifts and inheritances, is not a direct question about background checks, and carries a sales-only re-estimate of 14% to 22%. It is not used in copy.

## A4. Public support for universal background checks
*Used in: Section 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Adults who support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers (May 2023) | 86% |
| Adults who favor subjecting private sales and gun-show sales to background checks (April 2021) | 81%, including 70% of Republicans |

**Sources:** McCourtney Institute for Democracy Mood of the Nation Poll (APM Research Lab), Poll: A Majority of Americans Support Universal Background Checks, Gun Licensing and an Assault Weapons Ban, May 2023, https://www.apmresearchlab.org/motn/americans-views-on-gun-policy-background-checks-assault-weapons-bans-second-amendment; Pew Research Center, Amid a Series of Mass Shootings in the U.S., Gun Policy Remains Deeply Divisive, April 2021, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/04/20/amid-a-series-of-mass-shootings-in-the-u-s-gun-policy-remains-deeply-divisive/

**Notes.** For broader context, Pew in June 2023 found 64% of U.S. adults favor banning assault-style weapons and 66% favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (Pew Research Center, Americans' Views of Specific Gun Policy Proposals, June 2023, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-views-of-specific-gun-policy-proposals/). These figures are not used in the brief's copy.

## A5. Connecticut permit-to-purchase law
*Used in: executive summary; Section 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Change in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate in the first 10 years after the October 1995 permit-to-purchase law | -40% |
| Nonfirearm homicides in the same period | No evidence of a reduction |

**Source:** Rudolph KE, Stuart EA, Vernick JS, Webster DW, Association Between Connecticut's Permit-to-Purchase Handgun Law and Homicides, American Journal of Public Health, August 2015, https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2015.302703

**Notes.** Synthetic control method comparing Connecticut with a weighted combination of comparison states; the law requires a permit, issued contingent on a background check, before any handgun purchase. This is an observational study and shows association, not causal proof.

## A6. Mass shootings, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Section 4; fact sheet.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings in 2023 | 656 |
| People killed | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |
| Trend | 255 in 2013; 689 (record) in 2021; 647 in 2022; 656 in 2023 |

**Sources:** Gun Violence Archive, Mass Shootings Report, 2023, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/reports/year=2023; counts as reported in Axios, Mass Shootings Increased in 2023, January 2024, https://www.axios.com/2024/01/09/mass-shooting-gun-violence-us-2023, and The Trace, Gun Violence by the Numbers in 2023, December 2023, https://www.thetrace.org/2023/12/data-gun-violence-deaths-america/

**Notes (style sheet B5).** GVA defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter; the definition is in this appendix, not in body copy. GVA is an open-source incident archive, not a federal statistical dataset, and it counts injuries as well as deaths. For comparison, the AP/USA Today/Northeastern Mass Killing Database, which uses a different definition (four or more people killed, excluding the perpetrator, within 24 hours), counted the Lewiston shooting of Oct. 25, 2023 as the year's 36th mass killing, a partial-year figure (AP/USA Today/Northeastern University, Mass Killings Database, 2023, https://apnews.com/projects/mass-shooting-killings-united-states/). The two counts are not interchangeable.

**Named incidents in Section 4.** Parkland 2018 (AR-15-style M&P15 rifle; 17 students and educators killed) and Uvalde 2022 (AR-15-style rifle; 19 children and two teachers killed): U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Examples of Mass Shootings Involving Assault Weapons and/or Large Capacity Magazines, December 2022, https://www.congress.gov/117/meeting/house/115244/documents/HHRG-117-JU08-20221215-SD007.pdf. Lewiston 2023 (a .308 Ruger SFAR, an AR-style semiautomatic rifle; 18 rounds fired in 45 seconds at the first location; 18 people killed): Independent Commission to Investigate the Facts of the Tragedy in Lewiston, Final Report, August 2024, https://www.maine.gov/icl/sites/maine.gov.icl/files/2024-08/Final%20Report%20Of%20The%20Independent%20Commission%20To%20Investigate%20The%20Facts%20Of%20The%20Tragedy%20In%20Lewiston.pdf; AP News, Army, Police Missed Chances Before Maine Mass Shootings, Report Says, August 2024, https://apnews.com/article/final-report-lewiston-maine-mass-shooting-0db62e967dcb77fab976e4782a63baa5

## A7. Rifle share of gun murders (FBI)
*Used in: Section 4 (one sentence, per style sheet B6).*

| Year | Rifle murders | Share of all murders | Share of firearm murders |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 390 | 2.6% (of 15,195) | 3.6% (of 11,006) |
| 2018 | 297 | 2.1% (of 14,123) | 2.9% (of 10,265) |

**Source:** FBI, Crime in the United States 2018, Expanded Homicide Data Table 8: Murder Victims by Weapon, 2014-2018, 2018, https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2018/crime-in-the-u.s.-2018/tables/expanded-homicide-data-table-8.xls

**Notes (style sheet B6).** The FBI does not separately identify AR-style rifles; "rifles" covers all types. The brief's copy uses the 2018 share of firearm murders (2.9%). The research assistant's source table listed 2.6% (2017) and 2.8% (2018), which mix denominators; the percentages above are recomputed directly from FBI Table 8 counts, with denominators shown, and supersede the compilation.

## A8. The federal assault weapons ban and mass-shooting deaths
*Used in: executive summary; Section 4; fact sheet; stat card 4.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass-shooting fatalities during the 1994-2004 ban, relative to the periods before and after | 70% less likely |
| Mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides during the ban period | 9 fewer |
| Assault-rifle share of 501 fatalities in 44 mass shootings with four or more fatalities, 1981-2017 | 430 (85.8%; 95% CI, 82.8-88.9) |

**Source:** DiMaggio C, et al., Changes in US Mass Shooting Deaths Associated With the 1994-2004 Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Analysis of Open-Source Data, Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019, https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000002060

**Notes.** Open-source data (Mother Jones, Los Angeles Times and Stanford archives), incidents with four or more fatalities, 1981-2017; linear regression controlling for yearly trend. This is an observational pre-post design and shows association, not causal proof. The study uses "assault rifles"; see the terminology note at the top of this appendix.

## A9. High-capacity magazines in high-fatality mass shootings
*Used in: Section 4; Section 5, recommendation 2; fact sheet.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings with six or more deaths, 1990-2017 | 69 |
| Share involving large-capacity magazines | 44 (64%) |
| Average deaths with vs. without large-capacity magazines | 12 vs. 7 (62% higher mean death toll) |
| Incidence in states without bans vs. with bans | More than double; annual deaths more than triple |

**Source:** Klarevas L, Conner A, Hemenway D, The Effect of Large-Capacity Magazine Bans on High-Fatality Mass Shootings, 1990-2017, American Journal of Public Health, December 2019, https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2019.305311

**Notes.** Large-capacity magazine defined as a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds; state panel analysis, 1990-2017, controlling for 10 covariates with state fixed effects. The federal ban of 1994-2004 also covered new large-capacity magazines. Observational study; association, not causal proof.

## A10. Extreme-risk laws and firearm suicide
*Used in: Section 5, recommendation 4.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Indiana: firearm suicides in the 10 years after its risk-based seizure law took effect | -7.5% |
| Connecticut: firearm suicides in the post-Virginia Tech period, when enforcement increased | -13.7% |

**Source:** Kivisto AJ, Phalen PL, Effects of Risk-Based Firearm Seizure Laws in Connecticut and Indiana on Suicide Rates, 1981-2015, Psychiatric Services, August 2018, https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ps.201700250

**Notes.** Quasi-experimental synthetic control and difference-in-place designs, 50-state panel, 1981-2015. Effects were specific to firearm suicides; no comparable reduction in nonfirearm suicides. Connecticut's law (1999) was enforced much more actively after the 2007 Virginia Tech shooting. Extreme-risk (red flag) laws allow courts to order the temporary removal of firearms from people found to pose a danger to themselves or others.

## A11. Federal gun violence research funding
*Used in: Section 5, recommendation 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Dickey Amendment | 1996 (barred CDC funds from being used to advocate or promote gun control) |
| First dedicated federal research funding in more than two decades | $25 million for fiscal 2020, split evenly between CDC and NIH |

**Source:** The Trace, Congress Will Fund Gun Violence Research for First Time in Two Decades, December 2019, https://www.thetrace.org/2019/12/congress-gun-violence-research-budget-agreement-cdc-nih/

**Notes.** Dickey Amendment text: Pub. L. No. 104-208, 110 Stat. 3009-244 (1996). See also Congressional Research Service, The Dickey Amendment: In Brief, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF11371.web.html. The copy's "23 years" is the interval between the 1996 amendment and the December 2019 appropriations agreement.

---

*Prepared for Safer Communities Brief No. 9. Draft for editorial review; not for publication.*

Northgate Progress Institute | Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026

**The toll**

1. **46,728 Americans died by gun violence in 2023, one every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual total ever recorded.** (CDC WONDER, 2023, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025)

8. **Mass shootings with six or more deaths killed an average of 12 people when the shooter had a high-capacity magazine, versus 7 without one.** (Klarevas, Conner and Hemenway, American Journal of Public Health, 2019)

# Universal background checks and an assault weapons ban would save American lives, new NPI brief finds

WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026) — The Northgate Progress Institute today released "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," Safer Communities Brief No. 9, by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.

The brief documents the two federal gaps behind those numbers: an estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no background check, and the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004 with no replacement. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than in the periods before and after.

"The gaps in our gun laws are not accidents. They are choices, and in 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at NPI. "One in five recent gun acquisitions involved no background check at all. For the decade the assault weapons ban was in force, mass-shooting deaths were 70% less likely. Congress does not lack evidence. It lacks the will to use it."

The brief calls on Congress to pass universal background checks on every firearm sale and transfer, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban including a ban on high-capacity magazines, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and support state extreme-risk protection orders with implementation grants.

State evidence, the brief shows, is already in hand: Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in its firearm homicide rate, and extreme-risk laws were followed by firearm suicide reductions of 7.5% in Indiana and 13.7% in Connecticut.

A data appendix, a fact sheet for Hill offices and shareable stat cards accompany the release. The brief is available at [link to be added by editor].

## About the Northgate Progress Institute

The Northgate Progress Institute is a progressive policy think tank based in Washington, D.C. The Safer Communities series presents evidence-based policy briefs on gun violence prevention.

---

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield**, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Scheduled publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- The gaps in federal law are measurable and deadly. An estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no background check, and roughly half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- The evidence for action is in. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in the state's firearm homicide rate, and mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the decade the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the ban, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun. The final count was 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data.

Behind each of those numbers is a person: a parent at a kitchen table, a teenager at a bus stop, a coworker who did not come home. That is a loss the country has learned to absorb rather than stop. It shows up in every kind of community, in homes and on city blocks, at schools and workplaces, at grocery stores, birthday parties and family celebrations. The toll has held near record highs year after year, and it has touched every state. No comparable high-income country accepts anything like it, because none of them has to. Gun violence on this scale is not weather. It is the product of laws Congress wrote and of gaps Congress has declined to close.

## 2. Children and teens

The clearest measure of that failure is generational. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancers, according to the CDC.

The country did not arrive here by accident. Two open doors in federal law put guns in the wrong hands: a background-check requirement that stops at the storefront, and a legal market, restored after 2004, in assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that make mass shootings deadlier.

## 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every sale by a licensed firearms dealer since 1994. The Brady framework stops at the storefront door. In most states, a sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no record and no questions.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of that gap at 22%. In a national survey published in 2017 in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check. Among private-party sales, about half involved no check at all. In a country where 46,728 people died by gunfire in a single year, that gap is not a technicality. It is the on-ramp by which guns reach the very people the law already says should not have them.

A background check takes minutes, and it asks only whether the buyer falls into a category Congress has already barred from gun ownership: people convicted of serious crimes, domestic abusers and others the law disqualifies. The check is not an infringement on anyone Congress allows to own a gun. It is the system Congress built to enforce its own decisions, and it only works if it applies to every sale.

The checks work where they are actually required. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which places a background check on every handgun sale in the state, was followed by a 40% reduction in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable change in nonfirearm homicides.

The public is not waiting to be persuaded. In the May 2023 Mood of the Nation poll, 86% of American adults supported requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers. Pew Research Center found in April 2021 that 81% of Americans, including 70% of Republicans, favored extending checks to private sales and gun shows.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. The country knows these events by their place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the shooter was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of all kinds are used in a small share of the nation's gun murders, 2.9% of them in 2018 in FBI data, but they are concentrated in the deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 mass shootings with four or more fatalities recorded between 1981 and 2017, 430 were killed with assault rifles, 86% of the toll. The firepower drives the death count: of 69 mass shootings with six or more deaths between 1990 and 2017, 44 involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, compared with seven when the shooter did not have one. States without bans on the magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with them.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than in the periods before and after, and the ban period was associated with nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The law expired in 2004, and since then the annual count of mass shootings has more than doubled, from 255 in 2013 to 656 in 2023.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online loopholes that leave an estimated 22% of recent acquisitions unchecked and about half of private sales without a check.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's core protections, update its definitions to capture the variants marketed since 2004, and prohibit the high-capacity magazines that raise the average death toll in the deadliest attacks from seven victims to 12.

3. **Fund the science of gun safety.** Sustain and expand dedicated gun violence research funding at the CDC and the NIH. The first dedicated appropriation in more than two decades, $25 million for fiscal 2020, passed in December 2019, 23 years after the Dickey Amendment restricted federal gun violence research. A year in which 46,728 Americans die by gunfire should end that era of underfunding for good.

4. **Back state extreme-risk laws.** Provide planning and implementation grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people found to be a danger to themselves or others. In the first two states studied, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement began.

## Closing

The gaps this brief describes are the result of choices, and in 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives, including 2,566 children and teens. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban are not untested ideas. They are policies the country has already tried, measured and found to work, and they command broad public support. The evidence is assembled in this brief and its data appendix. What is missing is the vote.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield**, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Draft for editorial review | Scheduled publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- The gaps in federal law are measurable and deadly. An estimated 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no background check, and roughly half of private-party gun sales involve no check at all.
- The evidence for action is in. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in the state's firearm homicide rate, and mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the decade the federal assault weapons ban was in force. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the ban, fund the research and back state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Every 11 minutes in 2023, someone in America was killed with a gun. The final count was 46,728 people, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, according to CDC data.

Behind each of those numbers is a person: a parent at a kitchen table, a teenager at a bus stop, a coworker who did not come home. That is a loss the country has learned to absorb rather than stop. It shows up in every kind of community, in homes and on city blocks, at schools and workplaces, at grocery stores, birthday parties and family celebrations. The toll has held near record highs year after year, and it has touched every state. No comparable high-income country accepts anything like it, because none of them has to. Gun violence on this scale is not weather. It is the product of laws Congress wrote and of gaps Congress has declined to close.

## 2. Children and teens

The clearest measure of that failure is generational. In 2023, gunfire killed 2,566 American children and teens, an average of seven young people every day. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancers, according to the CDC.

The country did not arrive here by accident. Two open doors in federal law put guns in the wrong hands: a background-check requirement that stops at the storefront, and a legal market, restored after 2004, in assault weapons and the high-capacity magazines that make mass shootings deadlier.

## 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every sale by a licensed firearms dealer since 1994. The Brady framework stops at the storefront door. In most states, a sale arranged online, at a gun show or between strangers can proceed with no check, no record and no questions.

The best recent national estimate puts the size of that gap at 22%. In a national survey published in 2017 in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of gun owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check. Among private-party sales, about half involved no check at all. In a country where 46,728 people died by gunfire in a single year, that gap is not a technicality. It is the on-ramp by which guns reach the very people the law already says should not have them.

A background check takes minutes, and it asks only whether the buyer falls into a category Congress has already barred from gun ownership: people convicted of serious crimes, domestic abusers and others the law disqualifies. The check is not an infringement on anyone Congress allows to own a gun. It is the system Congress built to enforce its own decisions, and it only works if it applies to every sale.

The checks work where they are actually required. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which places a background check on every handgun sale in the state, was followed by a 40% reduction in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade, with no comparable change in nonfirearm homicides.

The public is not waiting to be persuaded. In the May 2023 Mood of the Nation poll, 86% of American adults supported requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers. Pew Research Center found in April 2021 that 81% of Americans, including 70% of Republicans, favored extending checks to private sales and gun shows.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those attacks killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more. The country knows these events by their place names: Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022, Lewiston in 2023. In each, the shooter was armed with an assault-style semiautomatic rifle. In Lewiston, the gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds.

Rifles of all kinds are used in a small share of the nation's gun murders, 2.9% in 2018, according to the FBI, but they are concentrated in the deadliest attacks. Of the 501 people killed in the 44 mass shootings with four or more fatalities recorded between 1981 and 2017, 430 were killed with assault rifles, 86% of the toll. The firepower drives the death count: of 69 mass shootings with six or more deaths between 1990 and 2017, 44 involved high-capacity magazines, and those attacks killed an average of 12 people, compared with seven when the shooter did not have one. States without bans on the magazines experienced high-fatality mass shootings at more than twice the rate of states with them.

The federal government has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and new high-capacity magazines. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than in the periods before and after, and the ban period was associated with nine fewer mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides. The law expired in 2004, and since then the annual count of mass shootings has more than doubled, from 255 in 2013 to 656 in 2023.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Extend the background-check requirement to every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online loopholes that leave an estimated 22% of recent acquisitions unchecked and about half of private sales without a check.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's core protections, update its definitions to capture the variants marketed since 2004, and prohibit the high-capacity magazines that raise the average death toll in the deadliest attacks from seven victims to 12.

3. **Fund the science of gun safety.** Sustain and expand dedicated gun violence research funding at the CDC and the NIH. The first dedicated appropriation in more than two decades, $25 million for fiscal 2020, passed in December 2019, 23 years after the Dickey Amendment restricted federal gun violence research. A year in which 46,728 Americans die by gunfire should end that era of underfunding for good.

4. **Back state extreme-risk laws.** Provide planning and implementation grants to states that enact and enforce extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people found to be a danger to themselves or others. In the first two states studied, Indiana saw firearm suicides fall 7.5% and Connecticut 13.7% after enforcement began.

## Closing

The gaps this brief describes are the result of choices, and in 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives, including 2,566 children and teens. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban are not untested ideas. They are policies the country has already tried, measured and found to work, and they command broad public support. The evidence is assembled in this brief and its data appendix. What is missing is the vote.
