# Data appendix: Closing the gaps (Safer Communities Brief No. 9)

Northgate Progress Institute | Draft for editorial review | Companion to brief.md
All figures used in the brief appear below, one table per figure, with source lines and notes. Per the publications style sheet, intent breakdowns, age ranges, definitions and methodology notes live in this appendix, not in body copy, the fact sheet or the stat cards.

**Terminology (style sheet A2).** House style uses "assault weapons" for the category defined in the author's outline, i.e., the semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity magazines covered by the federal assault weapons ban of 1994 (Public Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act), which took effect in September 1994 and expired in September 2004. Cited studies use their own terms ("assault rifles," "high-capacity" or "large-capacity" magazines); original wording is preserved in the tables below.

## A1. U.S. firearm deaths, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Sections 1, 3 and 5; closing; fact sheet; stat card 1.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Total firearm deaths | 46,728 (third-highest annual total ever recorded) |
| Firearm suicides | 27,300 (58% of total; record high) |
| Firearm homicides | 17,927 |
| Frequency | One death every 11 minutes |

**Source:** CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 2023 final data, https://wonder.cdc.gov/, as compiled in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

**Notes (style sheet B2).** The headline toll in body copy is total gun deaths; the intent breakdown appears here. Suicides have been the majority of U.S. gun deaths every year since 1995. Firearm homicides declined from their pandemic-era peak of 20,958 (2021) and 19,651 (2022) to 17,927 (2023); the overall 2023 total was still the third-highest ever recorded, and total gun deaths remained near the record set in 2021. CDC final mortality data come from death certificates and are released with a lag, so 2023 is the most recent year of final data. Rates elsewhere in this appendix are per 100,000 U.S. residents.

## A2. Children and teens, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Section 2; closing; fact sheet; stat card 2.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Firearm deaths, ages 1-17, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Rate, ages 1-17 | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Leading cause of death for this age group | Fourth consecutive year |
| Intent breakdown | Homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined or other 3% |

**Source:** CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 2023 final data, https://wonder.cdc.gov/, as compiled in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

**Notes (style sheet B3).** Body copy follows house phrasing, "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; the age range is ages 1-17, and firearms accounted for more deaths in this group than car crashes, overdoses or cancers. "An average of seven young people every day" (Section 2) is a derivation: 2,566 deaths across 365 days. A separate pooled estimate for ages 1-19 (5.9 per 100,000, 2021-2023, America's Health Rankings) is in the source tables but was not used in copy; flag to research if the editor wants it included.

## A3. Firearm acquisitions without a background check
*Used in: executive summary; Section 3; Section 5, recommendation 1; fact sheet; stat card 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Owners who acquired a firearm in the prior 2 years without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16% to 27%) |
| Private-party purchases acquired without a check | ~50% |

**Source:** Miller M, Hepburn L, Azrael D, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, February 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590

**Notes (style sheet B4).** 2015 national probability-based survey of 1,613 gun owners; "recent acquisition" means the most recent firearm obtained within the previous two years. The 22% figure is the house estimate for copy. An older and frequently misused figure, from the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook and Ludwig), found about 40% of recently acquired guns had not gone through a licensed dealer; that estimate includes gifts and inheritances, is not a direct question about background checks, and carries a sales-only re-estimate of 14% to 22%. It is not used in copy.

## A4. Public support for universal background checks
*Used in: Section 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Adults who support requiring background checks for all firearm sales and transfers (May 2023) | 86% |
| Adults who favor subjecting private sales and gun-show sales to background checks (April 2021) | 81%, including 70% of Republicans |

**Sources:** McCourtney Institute for Democracy Mood of the Nation Poll (APM Research Lab), Poll: A Majority of Americans Support Universal Background Checks, Gun Licensing and an Assault Weapons Ban, May 2023, https://www.apmresearchlab.org/motn/americans-views-on-gun-policy-background-checks-assault-weapons-bans-second-amendment; Pew Research Center, Amid a Series of Mass Shootings in the U.S., Gun Policy Remains Deeply Divisive, April 2021, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/04/20/amid-a-series-of-mass-shootings-in-the-u-s-gun-policy-remains-deeply-divisive/

**Notes.** For broader context, Pew in June 2023 found 64% of U.S. adults favor banning assault-style weapons and 66% favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (Pew Research Center, Americans' Views of Specific Gun Policy Proposals, June 2023, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-views-of-specific-gun-policy-proposals/). These figures are not used in the brief's copy.

## A5. Connecticut permit-to-purchase law
*Used in: executive summary; Section 3.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Change in Connecticut's firearm homicide rate in the first 10 years after the October 1995 permit-to-purchase law | -40% |
| Nonfirearm homicides in the same period | No evidence of a reduction |

**Source:** Rudolph KE, Stuart EA, Vernick JS, Webster DW, Association Between Connecticut's Permit-to-Purchase Handgun Law and Homicides, American Journal of Public Health, August 2015, https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2015.302703

**Notes.** Synthetic control method comparing Connecticut with a weighted combination of comparison states; the law requires a permit, issued contingent on a background check, before any handgun purchase. This is an observational study and shows association, not causal proof.

## A6. Mass shootings, 2023
*Used in: executive summary; Section 4; fact sheet.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings in 2023 | 656 |
| People killed | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |
| Trend | 255 in 2013; 689 (record) in 2021; 647 in 2022; 656 in 2023 |

For comparison, the AP/USA Today/Northeastern Mass Killing Database, which uses a different definition (four or more people killed, excluding the perpetrator, within 24 hours), counted the Lewiston shooting of Oct. 25, 2023 as the year's 36th mass killing, a partial-year figure (AP/USA Today/Northeastern University, Mass Killings Database, 2023, https://apnews.com/projects/mass-shooting-killings-united-states/). *Used in: Section 4 (one sentence, per style sheet B6).*

| Year | Rifle murders | Share of all murders | Share of firearm murders |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 390 | 2.6% (of 15,195) | 3.6% (of 11,006) |
| 2018 | 297 | 2.1% (of 14,123) | 2.9% (of 10,265) |

**Source:** FBI, Crime in the United States 2018, Expanded Homicide Data Table 8: Murder Victims by Weapon, 2014-2018, 2018, https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2018/crime-in-the-u.s.-2018/tables/expanded-homicide-data-table-8.xls

**Notes (style sheet B6).** The FBI does not separately identify AR-style rifles; "rifles" covers all types. The brief's copy uses the 2018 share of firearm murders (2.9%). The research assistant's source table listed 2.6% (2017) and 2.8% (2018), which mix denominators; the percentages above are recomputed directly from FBI Table 8 counts, with denominators shown, and supersede the compilation.

## A8. The federal assault weapons ban and mass-shooting deaths
*Used in: executive summary; Section 4; fact sheet; stat card 4.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass-shooting fatalities during the 1994-2004 ban, relative to the periods before and after | 70% less likely |
| Mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides during the ban period | 9 fewer |
| Assault-rifle share of 501 fatalities in 44 mass shootings with four or more fatalities, 1981-2017 | 430 (85.8%; 95% CI, 82.8-88.9) |

**Source:** DiMaggio C, et al., Changes in US Mass Shooting Deaths Associated With the 1994-2004 Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Analysis of Open-Source Data, Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019, https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000002060

**Notes.** Open-source data (Mother Jones, Los Angeles Times and Stanford archives), incidents with four or more fatalities, 1981-2017; linear regression controlling for yearly trend. This is an observational pre-post design and shows association, not causal proof. The study uses "assault rifles"; see the terminology note at the top of this appendix.

## A9. High-capacity magazines in high-fatality mass shootings
*Used in: Section 4; Section 5, recommendation 2; fact sheet.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings with six or more deaths, 1990-2017 | 69 |
| Share involving large-capacity magazines | 44 (64%) |
| Average deaths with vs. without large-capacity magazines | 12 vs. 7 (62% higher mean death toll) |
| Incidence in states without bans vs. with bans | More than double; annual deaths more than triple |

**Source:** Klarevas L, Conner A, Hemenway D, The Effect of Large-Capacity Magazine Bans on High-Fatality Mass Shootings, 1990-2017, American Journal of Public Health, December 2019, https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2019.305311

**Notes.** Large-capacity magazine defined as a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds; state panel analysis, 1990-2017, controlling for 10 covariates with state fixed effects. *Used in: Section 5, recommendation 4.*

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|

6. **Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over the law's first decade.** (Rudolph et al., American Journal of Public Health, 2015)

7. **Mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban than in the periods before and after it.** (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019)

8. **Mass shootings with six or more deaths killed an average of 12 people when the shooter had a high-capacity magazine, versus 7 without one.** (Klarevas, Conner and Hemenway, American Journal of Public Health, 2019)

# Universal background checks and an assault weapons ban would save American lives, new NPI brief finds

WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026) — The Northgate Progress Institute today released "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," Safer Communities Brief No. 9, by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, the third-highest annual toll ever recorded. Guns remained the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens for the fourth straight year.

The brief documents the gaps behind those numbers: an estimated 22% of recent gun acquisitions involved no background check, and the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004. During the ban years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely than before and after it.

"The gaps in our gun laws are not accidents. They are choices, and in 2023 they cost 46,728 American lives," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at NPI. "One in five recent gun acquisitions involved no background check. For the decade the assault weapons ban was in force, mass-shooting deaths were 70% less likely. Congress does not lack evidence. It lacks the will to use it."

The brief calls on Congress to pass universal background checks on every firearm sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, including high-capacity magazines, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and back state extreme-risk laws. The state evidence is in hand: Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% drop in its firearm homicide rate, and extreme-risk laws by firearm suicide reductions of 7.5% in Indiana and 13.7% in Connecticut.

A data appendix, fact sheet and stat cards accompany the release. Read the brief at [link].
